source.title: Return-to-Play in Sport: A Decision-based Model

paper.citation: Creighton D.W., Shrier I., Shultz R., Meeuwisse W.H., Matheson G.O. Return-to-Play in Sport: A Decision-based Model. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2010;20(5):379-385. doi:10.1097/JSM.0b013e3181f3c0fe.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can return-to-play decision making be organized into a clinically useful sequence that makes the inputs and judgment thresholds explicit? Participants: No participant sample; this is a conceptual review and model-development paper. Sport and level: Sport broadly, with examples across injuries, illnesses, positions, and levels of participation. Design: Narrative review and conceptual model development. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable.
paper.tldr: The model separates the decision into health status, participation risk, and decision modifiers rather than treating clearance as a single test result. Participation risk is informed by current health plus sport-risk modifiers such as position and the ability to protect the injury. Use the model as a structured decision record: document health evidence first, then sport-specific exposure risk, then external or contextual modifiers.
paper.methods: Design: Narrative review and conceptual model development. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable. Comparator: Not applicable. Measurements and outcomes: Organization of factors used in return-to-play decisions. Analysis: Synthesis of the literature into a three-step decision model.
paper.findings: The model separates the decision into health status, participation risk, and decision modifiers rather than treating clearance as a single test result. Participation risk is informed by current health plus sport-risk modifiers such as position and the ability to protect the injury. The acceptable-risk threshold can differ between decision makers and change with context, making the value judgment important to document.
paper.limitations: This is a conceptual model, not a validated prediction rule, and it supplies neither quantitative criteria nor weights for its components. Interpretation: The framework can improve transparency, but it cannot determine whether a particular athlete is medically ready or estimate reinjury probability.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the model as a structured decision record: document health evidence first, then sport-specific exposure risk, then external or contextual modifiers. Do not let schedule pressure or stakeholder preference masquerade as biological recovery. The framework is most useful for clarifying who owns each judgment and why reasonable professionals may reach different thresholds.
